items.followUp: What was the main idea of Rutherford’s nuclear model of the atom?

rubric.why: The definition must describe the positive matter and the embedded electrons.
rubric.description: Describes the atom as positive matter with electrons embedded in it.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that electrons are embedded in a positively charged sphere or matter, like plums in pudding.

rubric.why: J. J. Thomson proposed the plum pudding model.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for naming J. J. Thomson.

modelAnswer: The plum pudding theory describes the atom as a positively charged sphere with electrons embedded in it, like plums in a pudding.
It was proposed by J. J. Thomson.

items.followUp: Write any two properties of cathode rays.

rubric.why: Positive rays have several characteristic properties; any one valid property earns this mark.
rubric.description: States one valid property of positive rays.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for one correct property, such as being positively charged, travelling in straight lines, or being deflected towards the negative plate.

rubric.why: The question asks for two properties, so a second distinct property is required.
rubric.description: States a second distinct valid property of positive rays.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for another correct property not already used for the first mark.

modelAnswer: Positive rays consist of positively charged particles.
They are deflected towards the negative plate in an electric field.

items.followUp: What are the blocks of the periodic table called, and how are they arranged?

rubric.why: Periods are the horizontal rows of the periodic table.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying periods as horizontal rows.

rubric.why: Groups are the vertical columns of the periodic table.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying groups as vertical columns.

modelAnswer: Groups are the vertical columns in the periodic table.
Periods are the horizontal rows in the periodic table.

items.followUp: Why does atomic radius generally decrease from left to right across a period?

rubric.why: Across a period, nuclear charge increases while added electrons enter the same principal shell.
rubric.description: Explains the increase in nuclear charge across a period.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that nuclear charge or proton number increases while electrons are added to the same shell.

rubric.why: The stronger attraction holds the outer electron more tightly, so more energy is needed to remove it.
rubric.description: Links stronger nuclear attraction to increased ionization energy.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that outer electrons are attracted more strongly and require more energy to remove.

modelAnswer: From left to right in a period, nuclear charge increases while the added electrons enter the same shell.
The stronger attraction between the nucleus and the outer electron makes the electron harder to remove, so ionization energy increases.

items.followUp: Why does the shielding effect increase down a group?

rubric.why: Shielding is caused by electrons in shells between the nucleus and the outer electrons.
rubric.description: Identifies the electrons responsible for shielding.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that inner-shell electrons cause the effect.

rubric.why: Inner electrons screen the outer electrons from the nucleus and reduce the nuclear attraction experienced by them.
rubric.description: Defines the effect on outer electrons.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for explaining that the inner electrons screen or reduce the nucleus's attraction to outer electrons.

modelAnswer: The shielding effect is the reduction in the attraction between the nucleus and outer-shell electrons caused by inner-shell electrons.
The inner-shell electrons screen the outer electrons from the nuclear charge.

items.followUp: How many elements are present in the 3rd and 4th periods?

rubric.why: The first period contains two elements.
rubric.description: Gives the number of elements in the first period.

rubric.why: The second period contains eight elements.
rubric.description: Gives the number of elements in the second period.

items.followUp: Write any two properties of ionic compounds.

rubric.why: Covalent compounds have several characteristic physical properties; any one valid property earns this mark.
rubric.description: States one valid property of covalent compounds.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for one correct property, such as low melting or boiling points or poor electrical conductivity.

rubric.why: The question asks for two properties, so a second distinct property is required.
rubric.description: States a second distinct valid property of covalent compounds.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for another correct property not already used for the first mark.

modelAnswer: Covalent compounds usually have low melting and boiling points.
They are generally poor conductors of electricity.

items.followUp: Define a double covalent bond and give one example.

rubric.why: A triple covalent bond involves the sharing of three pairs of electrons.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that three pairs of electrons are shared between two atoms.

rubric.why: A nitrogen molecule is a standard example containing a triple covalent bond.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for giving N₂ (nitrogen molecule) as an example.

modelAnswer: A triple covalent bond is formed when two atoms share three pairs of electrons.
A nitrogen molecule, N₂, contains a triple covalent bond.
